periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem — Listening, Reciting, and Exploring

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us recite (pp.104–105): teacher-led read-aloud and choral recitation of the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem 'Night' (pp.104–105) aloud with expression, inviting students to follow in their textbooks. Teacher pauses at the end of each stanza to let students absorb the images of the sinking sun and the darkening world.

Let us recite — ("choral read-aloud of the full poem"). The class reads the poem aloud together two or three times; teacher models the rhyming pairs bright/night, still/hill, sleep/peep and encourages students to feel the rhythm as they recite.

Let us recite — ("repeated reading: pairs practise aloud"). In pairs, students take turns reading the poem to each other; teacher moves around, listening for fluency and gently correcting pronunciation of words such as 'distant', 'sinks', and 'shining'.

Let us recite — ("whole-class share-back and appreciation"). Two or three volunteers read the poem aloud to the class; teacher draws brief attention to the feeling of wonder in the child-narrator's voice and the image of the sun as a companion that leaves and returns.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem carries a gentle, wonder-filled tone: the child watches the sun sink behind a hill and then falls asleep, waking to find it shining again. Encourage students to use a soft, curious voice that matches this mood rather than a flat reading. Rhyming pairs bright/night and sleep/peep are key entry points for noticing how sound shapes meaning in poetry.

periods.activity_title: Talking About the Sun, the Sky, and the Night

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think (p.106): guided discussion on where the sun goes, what the sky holds, and a sunless day.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the poem 'Night' aloud once (pp.104–105) to bring the sun's journey back to mind. Students listen with books open and join in quietly on the last two lines.

Let us think — A. ("answer questions on the sun's journey"). Teacher poses the three questions from section A one at a time: where the sun goes at day's end, which living and non-living things need the sun and why, and what else the child-narrator might see when looking up at the sky. Students respond orally; teacher invites two or three answers per question and extends them with a follow-up word.

Let us think — B. ("think-and-talk on sunrise colours and night sky"). Teacher guides discussion through questions B1–B3 — the colours of sunrise and sunset, what the sky looks like at night, and how waking up in the morning feels. Students share in pairs first, then with the class; teacher links their answers back to the poem's images of darkness, stillness, and the sun shining down.

Let us think — B. ("imagining a sunless day — whole-class talk"). Teacher poses the final thought-experiment: imagine a day when the sun never comes out, and invite students to talk about what that day would be like. Students speak freely; teacher keeps the conversation grounded in the poem's idea of the world growing 'dark and still'.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read and recited the poem together, students now use it as a springboard for personal observation and imagination. Encourage them to draw on real experience — colours they have actually seen at sunrise or sunset, stars and the moon at night — rather than generic answers. The sunless-day question opens creative thinking; accept a wide range of ideas as long as students can explain their reasoning briefly.

periods.activity_title: Consonant Blends and Sky Words — Phonics and Word-Building

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (pp.107–108): oral blend-and-say drill for sp-, st-, sk- words.
Let us learn A (p.108): read and circle words that belong in the sky.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn B (p.108): add 'Sun' to each word to make a compound word and write it in the space given.

time_bands.activity: Let us speak — ("sp-, st-, sk- blend-and-say drill"). Teacher writes the blends sp, st, sk on the board and reminds students that the poem's companion sentence 'I spy a few stars in the sky' contains all three. Teacher says each word from the list (Star, Storm, Store, Stain, Stick, Stair, Spoon, Splash, Spin, Skin, Skate, Sky) and students repeat, emphasising the initial blend; teacher then calls on individuals to say one word each.

Let us speak — ("sorting sp- / st- / sk- words in small groups"). Students work in groups of three; each group sorts the twelve words into three blend columns in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, checking that students are identifying the opening blend correctly and are not confusing st- and sk-.

Let us learn A — ("read the word list and circle sky words"). Teacher reads the full word list aloud with the class (Stars, Storm, Store, Stain, Sun, Bicycle, Moon, Rain, Clouds, Flowers, Rainbow, Monkeys, Computer, Shoes), then students work individually in their textbooks to circle only the words that can actually be found in the sky. After a brief individual attempt, students share their answers; teacher confirms the sky words and briefly explains any that students find uncertain, such as 'storm' and 'rainbow'.

Quick oral close — students say one sky word each around the class in a fast chain, starting from any student; teacher ends with 'And the sun shines down on all of them!' to echo the poem's close and consolidate the session.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem opens with the sp-blend sentence 'I spy a few stars in the sky', which links phonics directly to the text students already know by ear. Students at Grade III often blend the consonants separately rather than as a single onset; model the smooth run sp-, st-, sk- clearly before the drill. For the sky-word task, accept brief reasoning for borderline words such as 'storm' and 'rain' — the goal is word recognition in context, not a rigid list.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for blend display

periods.activity_title: Playing 'I Spy' — Observation, Clues, and Vocabulary in Action

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do (p.107): whole-class 'I Spy' game — each child takes a turn as the Spy and gives colour or shape clues.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces 'I Spy' by modelling one round: 'I spy with my little eye something that is yellow.' Students look around the room and guess; teacher confirms the correct answer. Teacher explains the two roles — the Spy who gives clues, and the guessers — and sets the rule that the Spy gives colour clues first and may add a second clue if needed.

Let us do — ("class 'I Spy' game — rotating spy role"). Students take turns being the Spy in a brisk classroom round; each Spy says 'I spy with my little eye something that is …' and provides one clue. The child who guesses correctly becomes the next Spy. Teacher keeps the pace lively and nudges students who hesitate by asking 'What colour is it? What shape?' to scaffold their clue-giving.

Let us do — ("sky-themed spy round"). Teacher invites one final round in which the Spy must choose something that could be in the sky — drawing on the vocabulary from the poem and the word work on sky words (sun, clouds, moon, stars, rainbow). This links the game back to the poem's images and consolidates the vocabulary from across the chapter.

Brief whole-class reflection: teacher asks students to share one word they used as a clue today that also appears in the poem or the sky-word list. Two or three students respond; teacher closes by reciting the poem's final lines together — 'And when my eyes open, / I see the Sun is / shining down on me' — as a quiet, celebratory end to the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'I Spy' activity is rooted in the poem's opening image of the child-narrator observing the sky and wondering. Encourage students to use descriptive language beyond basic colours — shape, size, or texture — when giving a second clue. The sky-themed final round ties the playful game back to the poem's vocabulary and consolidates the chapter as a whole.
materials: The classroom environment itself (objects visible in the room)

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 104 beginning "The sun that shines all day so bright". Which two words at the end of those first two lines rhyme with each other?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be matching the last word of line 1 with the last word of line 3, confusing which lines form the rhyming pair.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be focusing on repeated words in the poem rather than on end-sound rhyme.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be pairing words that appear near each other rather than listening for matching end sounds.

items.item_stem: The poem on page 104 says the day 'begins to peep'. In your own words, say or write one sentence explaining what you think this means.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The day 'begins to peep' means that daylight slowly starts to appear, as if the new day is quietly peeking in while the child is still waking up.

items.source_lo: Student responds to questions, describes experiences, and imagines scenarios using guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sun's disappearance at night, sky observations, sunrise/sunset colours, imagining a sunless day.
items.item_stem: The poem says the sun sinks behind a distant hill and the world grows dark and still. Which of the following best describes what happens to the world when the sun disappears at night?

options.text: The child stays awake all night waiting for the sun.
The sun goes behind a hill and comes back immediately.
The world becomes dark and quiet when the sun goes down.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is true: the poem clearly states 'all the world grows dark and still' when the sun sinks. Statements 2 and 3 are false: the poem shows the child going to sleep and waking to find the sun returned, not an immediate return or a sleepless night.

items.item_stem: The child in the poem wonders and observes the sky. Talk about what you see in the sky at different times of day — morning, afternoon, and night. Use at least two sky things in your answer.

expected_elements: Names at least two sky objects or phenomena.
Links observation to a time of day.

items.item_stem: Match each 'I Spy' clue to the object it is most likely describing.
items.visual_stimulus:
I Spy Clue | Object
"I spy something round and bright in the daytime sky." | Moon
"I spy something white and fluffy floating high up." | Sun
"I spy something silver and twinkling at night." | Cloud
"I spy something pale and round that glows at night." | Star

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Round and bright daytime – Sun; white and fluffy floating – Cloud; silver and twinkling at night – Star; pale and round glowing at night – Moon

"I spy something white and fluffy floating high up."

items.item_stem: Be the Spy! Choose one thing you would see in the sky at night — something from the poem or from your own knowledge. Say your 'I Spy' clue aloud and explain why you chose that clue.
